1.content: Create a native desktop app with Go and open your first window.
1.keywords: install create cli window bun macos

2.content: macOS 14 or later Go 1.23 or later Bun 1.4 or later Xcode Command Line Tools ( xcode-select --install ) macOS is the supported target today.

3.content: init writes the project and installs dependencies. Omit --language to choose Go, TypeScript, or Rust interactively.

4.content: main.go starts the app with native.Run and opens a window. Pass a component function to WindowOptions.Component . The component returns the UI for that window. OnReopen opens a window again when the user clicks the Dock icon and none are visible.

5.content: dev rebuilds your Go code and relaunches the app as you edit. fmt wraps long UI calls. build writes a packaged app under dist/ .

6.content: Write components . Keep them in sync with signals . Add styles and layout .

7.content: The files in a QuickGUI Go project and how to configure them. A Go project keeps application code in a Go module and development commands in a small Bun package.

8.content: Commit go.sum after resolving dependencies. Split larger apps into ordinary Go packages.

9.content: main.go starts native.Run and opens windows. A component is a function that returns *ui.Element . Return the UI you build — do not create views and ignore them.

10.content: entry is the Go package to build. The config file is for the CLI; it is not loaded by the running app. You can use quickgui.toml instead: The CLI reads quickgui.toml before quickgui.config.ts . Pass --config configs/dev.toml to choose a file. Quote version values, for example version = "..." . The application icon comes from resources/icon.png . Extra files can be listed in resources . Bundle custom fonts with fonts . See App Icon and Bundled Resources .

11.content: github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/native — windows and platform APIs github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/ui — components and styles github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/reactive — owners and contexts used by advanced code @quickgui/cli is a development dependency. To share your own components, see Authoring Extensions .

12.content: dev reloads when you change Go source or the config file.

13.content: Write components, compose children, and use the built-in control set. Write a function that returns *ui.Element . Start with View , Text , and Button , then compose the rest of the control set the same way.

14.content: Pass ordinary Go values. If an argument reads a signal, that binding stays live after the function returns — you do not need extra annotations. Structs work the same way. Updating quantity changes the text; LineItem stays mounted. Start containers with ui.View() and append content with .Child(...) or .Children(...) .

15.content: View , Text , Button , and Input cover most layout and text. Chain styles, properties, and handlers on the same element. The optional extensions/editor package adds the Rust-core Editor , CodeBlock , and DiffView surfaces without CGO or another native library. The optional extensions/markdown package adds retained Markdown , including streaming reconciliation and CodeBlock rendering.

16.content: Create an instance, then compose its named parts. Strings work as children. Configure behavior on the instance and styles on its parts. Nest parts the way you nest any other children.

17.content: Pass the current value and write the next value from the change callback. Create each instance inside the component that owns it.

18.content: The component reference covers forms, overlays, menus, tables, trees, and more. Run the gallery from this repository:

19.content: Apply styles on the part itself, or share a ui.Style() value: Adding OnClick keeps the part’s default action. Call PreventDefault() on OnClickEvent when you need to cancel it.

20.content: Keep UI in sync with signals, memos, effects, and batched updates. A component function runs once when its window (or parent) mounts. Signals keep text and properties up to date without rebuilding the whole tree.

21.content: Create a signal with ui.CreateSignal . Read it in text and properties: ui.Text("Count: ", count()) , .Width(width()) . Event handlers batch writes automatically. initial := count() is a snapshot. Read the signal again later when the value should stay live. You can also pass a signal as a child: ui.Text("Count: ", count) keeps the prefix and updates only the number. Custom components take ordinary int , string , and struct arguments. LineItem(product, quantity()) stays subscribed to quantity .

22.content: Use ui.CreateMemo for a value computed from other signals.

23.content: Use ui.CreateEffect for work outside the tree, such as a subscription or a window title. It runs after mount and again when a value it read changes. ui.OnCleanup runs before the next execution and when the component goes away. Update text and properties directly. Do not rebuild UI inside an effect.

24.content: Click handlers already batch writes. Wrap related writes elsewhere in ui.Batch so observers see one result. ui.Untrack reads a signal without subscribing. Read and write signals on the UI goroutine; use ui.Async or native.Dispatch to deliver background results.

25.content: Show and hide content, render lists, and work with the current window. A component builds its UI when it mounts. Use ui.Show and ui.For when children should appear, disappear, or reorder as state changes.

26.content: Every component returns *ui.Element . Pass children with .Child(...) or .Children(...) . Return ui.Fragment(...) for several siblings without a wrapper. A plain Go if or for runs only while the component is being built. It will not update later.

27.content: Use ui.Show to mount or remove children from state.

28.content: Use ui.For for a list that can change. Give each row a stable, unique key — a database ID, not its index. ui.KeyedFor also gives the row an accessor to the current item. Pass a new slice when you edit data. Mutating the stored slice in place does not notify subscribers. For long lists, use VirtualList or Table .

29.content: Each window has its own component root. Closing the window disposes its UI and effects. Register cleanup with ui.OnCleanup . ui.Async runs work off the UI goroutine, delivers the result back, and cancels if the component is gone.

30.content: Capture native.CurrentWindow() while the component is mounting, then use that handle in callbacks.

31.content: Run quickgui test from the app module. quickgui fmt --check checks formatting. The app is a Go executable, so the usual Go debugger and stack traces use your source files.

32.content: Lay out and style views with Flexbox, Grid, and interaction states. Chain style methods on elements or on ui.Style() . Append children with .Child(...) or .Children(...) , and reuse a style with .Style(shared) .
32.keywords: style layout flexbox grid color hover

33.content: Later values override the same property. Lengths are logical pixels; strings also accept percentages. Helpers such as .FlexCol() , .P4() , .GridCols(3) , and .RoundedLg() match the TypeScript presets.

34.content: .Style(base).Style(overrides) applies declarations in order. Use .Merge(...) to combine reusable builders.

35.content: ui.Style() returns a value. Methods return a new value, so a shared style is never mutated. Assign the result when you derive a variation. .When(condition, style) applies extra styles while the condition is true. For a reactive condition, pass a getter: .When(selected, ui.Style().Bg("#2563eb")) . Passing width() during setup captures the current number; pass width (the getter) when it should stay live.

36.content: .Flex() , .FlexRow() , or .FlexCol() start a flex layout. Give scrolling children .MinHeight(0) or .MinWidth(0) so they can shrink.

38.content: Typography inherits to children. Colors accept hex, rgb() / rgba() , or packed RGBA values. Padding and borders do not inherit.

39.content: Use .Hover(...) , .Active(...) , .FocusStyle(...) , .DisabledStyle(...) , and .SelectedStyle(...) . Add .Transition(...) on the base style to animate paint changes. See Transitions & Animation .

40.hierarchy: Styling & Layout › Groups and named group hover
40.content: .Group(true) marks an unnamed group; .Group("card") names it. .GroupHover(...) follows the nearest ancestor group. .GroupHoverNamed("card", ...) follows the nearest ancestor with that name. .GroupActive(...) and .FocusWithin(...) work the same way for pressed and focused groups. These states accept paint properties; they cannot set the cursor.

41.content: Build text fields, checkboxes, radios, and select controls. Keep field values in signals and write accepted changes back from callbacks.
41.keywords: input field checkbox radio select events

42.content: ui.Input and ui.TextArea are native text editors. Bind Value and update it from OnInput . OnSubmit handles Return in a single-line input.

43.content: Field groups a label, control, description, and error. Drive Required , Invalid , and ValidationMessage from your own state. See Field for validation modes.

44.content: Checkboxes accept bool or mixed state. Radio groups keep one value; checkbox and toggle groups can keep several. Disabled and read-only are separate.

45.content: Select chooses from a list. Combobox mixes typing and selection. Autocomplete accepts free-form input. Multiple selection uses Values and OnValuesChange .

46.content: Buttons take OnClick(func() { ... }) . Use OnClickEvent when you need *native.Event . Compound callbacks include the typed value and, when relevant, the event. Keep UI updates on the UI goroutine; use ui.Async for background work.

47.content: Show popovers, dialogs, and operating-system file pickers. Use a QuickGUI overlay for app-styled content, or a system dialog for file picking and alerts.
47.keywords: popover dialog overlay alert file picker

48.content: A popover has a trigger and a popup. The side is a preference; placement flips if it would overflow.

49.content: Build modal content under Portal . Title and Description name the dialog for accessibility. AlertDialog is for confirmations.

50.content: SystemPopover opens a native child window, which can extend past the owner window’s edge.

51.content: Capture the parent window while rendering, then pass it to the request. A canceled open panel sets Canceled: true .

52.content: Declare routes, nested layouts, and in-app navigation. Declare routes, render the match in the current window, and navigate with links or UseRouter .
52.keywords: router route layout outlet navigation history parameters

53.content: Use ui.Route for pages and ui.Layout for shared chrome. ui.Outlet is where the matched child renders.

54.content: Wrap related routes in ui.Layout . Navigation between sibling routes keeps the layout mounted, so its local state survives.

55.content: ui.UseRouter() exposes Navigate , Replace , Back , and Forward . ui.Link declares a target. Push adds a history entry; replace updates the current one.

56.content: Read path parameters with ui.UseParams , query values with ui.UseSearchParams , and the current location with ui.UseLocation . Read them when you display the value so the text stays current. A :name segment captures one path parameter.

57.content: Animate hover, color, and opacity, and play GIF or WebP images. Animate style changes with .Transition(...) . The component does not rerun for each frame.
57.keywords: transition animation hover opacity gif webp

58.content: Put the transition on the base style so it applies when the pointer enters and leaves. The same declaration works with Active , Focus , Expanded , and DragOver .

59.content: Change the target with a signal or .When . Keep the node mounted while it animates. Reversing mid-transition continues from the current visible value.

60.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Timing and frame rate
60.content: Use ui.TransitionDeclaration when several properties share one timing. Field Usage .TransitionProperty(...) Property names, as a comma-separated string or []string . .TransitionDuration(...) A number of milliseconds, a time.Duration , or "180ms" / "0.18s" . Durations are limited to 0–10 seconds. .TransitionEasing(...) "linear" , "ease" , "ease-in" , "ease-out" , or "ease-in-out" . .TransitionMaxFps(...) Optional frame-rate cap. Omit it to follow the display. A node has one duration, easing, and frame-rate cap for all selected properties. Delays, cubic-bezier() , and per-property timings are not supported. ui.Style().Transition(180 * time.Millisecond) animates background, border, and text colors. "all" includes every supported paint property. "none" removes the shorthand.

61.content: Transition name Style method background-color or background .BackgroundColor(...) or a solid .Background(...) border-color .BorderColor(...) border-width .BorderWidth(...) border-radius .BorderRadius(...) color .TextColor(...) opacity .Opacity(...) transform .Transform(...) box-shadow .BoxShadow(...) Width, height, padding, and gradient stops do not interpolate. For a sliding switch thumb, use .Transform("translateX(20px)") with .Transition("transform 160ms ease-out") .

62.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Mounting and reduced motion
62.content: A transition animates a change on an existing node. ui.Show removes children immediately; it does not wait for a fade-out. Opacity zero still receives layout and input. For dialogs, EnterDuration and ExitDuration control how long closing content stays mounted. See Dialog . Transitions follow the system Reduce Motion setting. Set native.WindowOptions.ReduceMotion to override it for one window.

63.content: Pass a GIF or WebP path to ui.Image . Playback follows the file; you do not need a timer. Package files with the CLI resources option. See Bundled Resources and Image .

64.content: Open windows and use menus, clipboard, dialogs, and file watching. Call native.Run once from main . Its startup callback creates windows and registers application handlers.
64.keywords: window menu clipboard WatchFiles Dispatch Async

65.content: native.NewWindow creates a window with its own component. Closing the window disposes that UI. Capture native.CurrentWindow() while constructing a component if a later callback needs the window handle. Handle the Dock icon with native.App.OnReopen so a new window opens when none are visible.

66.hierarchy: Windows & Native Services › Commands and services
66.content: Use the typed native APIs for dialogs, clipboard, shell, appearance, menus, notifications, and other platform features. Operations that return a result use a completion callback — handle errors there instead of blocking. Tray icons are covered in Tray Icon . For background work, ui.Async cancels when its component is disposed. native.Dispatch delivers a result back to the UI goroutine. Read and write signals only there. Independent native packages use native.InvokeExtension and native.OpenExtension . See Authoring Extensions .

67.hierarchy: Windows & Native Services › Events and file watching
67.content: native.WatchFiles(paths, changed, ready) uses operating-system notifications and returns a stop function. Register the stop function with ui.OnCleanup for component-owned watchers. Prefer a native event or watcher over polling.

68.content: Embed real SwiftUI controls inside a Go application. ui.SwiftUI embeds real macOS controls in a Go application. Ordinary QuickGUI components work without it.

69.content: Create controls inside ui.SwiftUI.Host . The host is the native view boundary and can size itself from its content.

70.content: Button, Slider, Toggle, ProgressView, Stepper, TextField, SecureField, Picker, SegmentedControl, DatePicker, ColorPicker, and Gauge. They look and behave like the system controls.

71.content: Bind a signal and store the value from the native callback. A SwiftUI control and a QuickGUI view can share the same signal. DatePicker uses Unix timestamps in milliseconds.

72.content: MatchContents: true sizes both axes from the control. Use ui.SwiftUIMatchContents{Vertical: true} for an intrinsic height and set the width yourself.

73.content: SwiftUI hosting requires macOS. Appearance can vary with the operating-system version.

74.content: Style SwiftUI controls and nest QuickGUI content inside them. Modifiers style native SwiftUI controls. Reverse hosting puts QuickGUI content inside SwiftUI.

75.content: Pass modifier factories through Modifiers . Available factories include ButtonStyle, ButtonBorderShape, ControlSize, LabelStyle, Tint, and Disabled.

76.content: On supported systems, ui.SwiftUI.ButtonStyle("glass") requests the system glass button. macOS chooses the final look.

77.content: ui.SwiftUI.QuickGUIHostView hosts a QuickGUI subtree. Give it a size and declare children in the callback.

78.content: The SwiftUI popover uses a native trigger. Its content can host QuickGUI children.

79.content: The host appears after the owner window is shown and closes when it is removed. Declare reverse-hosted children inside the callback so they belong to that embedded surface.

80.content: Use resources/icon.png as the packaged application icon, or change the window or Dock icon at runtime. The packaged application icon is the image Finder, the Dock, the Windows taskbar, Start Menu, and Linux desktop launchers show for your app. Put a PNG at resources/icon.png . You can also change a window icon or the macOS Dock icon while the app is running.
80.keywords: icon icns ico dock taskbar png

81.content: Add a square PNG that is at least 256×256 pixels at resources/icon.png . 1024×1024 is a good source. quickgui build resizes it to every size macOS, Windows, and Linux need. The CLI writes .icns for macOS, .ico for the Windows installer, and the Freedesktop hicolor sizes for Linux. Development reloads skip generated containers; production builds and a configured macos.icon still install an icon. Optional resources/icon.iconset/icon_<n>x<n>.png files replace a generated size with a hand-drawn one. That folder is a build input and is not copied into the packaged app. Set icon in the CLI config only when the source PNG lives somewhere other than resources/icon.png .

82.content: Use these when you already have a platform container: resources/icon.icns is used on macOS when macos.icon is omitted. resources/icon.ico is used by the NSIS installer when windows.icon is omitted. linux.icon is a square PNG used when both resources/icon.png and icon are omitted. macos.icon must be an .icns . windows.icon is an .ico . These config paths override the files in resources/ . Document-type icons are a basename inside the packaged resources. See Bundled Resources .

83.hierarchy: App Icon › Window and Dock icons
83.content: The packaged icon is the application identity. A window can show a different image on Windows and X11: iconPath is an absolute filesystem path. Join it from GetPaths as shown in Bundled Resources . After the window exists, call window.SetIcon(source) or window.ClearIcon() . On macOS, windows do not have their own icon. Use native.Desktop.SetDockIcon(&native.ImageSource{Path: iconPath}) to replace the Dock image for this process. Pass nil to restore the bundled icon. Menu-bar and notification-area icons are a different image. See Tray Icon .

84.content: Target Sizes macOS .icns 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024 Windows .ico 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 128, 256 Linux hicolor 16, 32, 48, 64, 128, 256, 512 Every listed size is generated from the source PNG. The source must be square, at least 256×256, and at most 16 MiB.

85.content: Add a menu-bar or notification-area icon, and mark macOS template images by filename or flag. A tray icon lives in the macOS menu bar, the Windows notification area, or a Linux StatusNotifierItem host. Put the artwork in resources/ and create the icon after startup. This is separate from the packaged App Icon .
85.keywords: tray menubar status template Template.png notification

86.hierarchy: Tray Icon › Create a tray icon
86.content: Ship a small PNG with the app, then create the icon from its packaged path: Tray.Create assigns an id. Call tray.Update , tray.ShowMenu , or tray.Destroy on that handle. native.Tray is supported on macOS, Windows, and Linux. A 22×22 PNG is a good 1× source. Draw a 44×44 companion as trayTemplate@2x.png when you want a retina menu-bar image.

87.content: On macOS, a template image is a monochrome mask. AppKit recolors it for the menu bar's light, dark, and highlighted appearances using only the alpha channel. A filename whose stem ends in Template , optionally followed by @2x or @3x , is treated as a template: trayTemplate.png and statusTemplate@2x.png match. emailTemplateIcon.png does not. Use native.TemplateImage(path) or set ImageSource.Template when the name does not follow that convention, or to force the flag off: The same ImageSource field applies to window icons, Dock icons, about-panel icons, and menu item icons. Other platforms keep the flag and ignore it.

88.content: The tray menu is a native context menu. Action items call Click . Listen for click , double-click , enter , move , leave , menu-item , and scroll on OnEvent . ShowMenu opens the menu at the cursor on macOS and Windows. Linux hosts own menu presentation and reject that call.

89.content: Platform Host Template images ShowMenu macOS Menu bar extra Recolored by AppKit Supported Windows Notification area Ignored Supported Linux StatusNotifierItem Ignored Unsupported Desktop.GetSupport reports TrayIcons and ProgrammableTrayPopup . Keep at most 32 tray icons.

90.content: Ship files in resources/ and load them from the packaged resource directory. Put application files that are not compiled into the executable in a resources/ directory: images, templates, JSON, and other data. The CLI copies that directory’s contents into the packaged app. The running app reads them from the resource directory, which does not depend on the launch working directory. Custom fonts are a separate option. See Fonts .

91.content: Each file keeps its path relative to resources/ . resources/hero.png is installed as hero.png . resources/copy/template.txt is installed as copy/template.txt . Destination names must not replace reserved names such as fonts , AppIcon.icns , quickgui.json , or the host shared library. quickgui dev and quickgui build both stage these files. A missing extra path listed in config fails the build. The resources/ directory itself is optional.

92.content: Use the resources config option to merge extra files or folders into the same packaged directory. Each extra path is copied under its basename. Do not list the project resources/ folder here; it is included automatically. legal/NOTICE.txt is installed as NOTICE.txt . vendor/data is installed as data/ .

93.content: Platform Resource directory macOS .app Contents/Resources Linux AppDir, AppImage, and .deb Next to the executable ( usr/bin ) Windows installer Next to the executable in $INSTDIR Join packaged names onto ResourceDir at runtime; do not read from the project tree or the current working directory.

94.content: Ask the host for paths after native.Run is ready, then join the packaged name: ui.Image accepts that filesystem path. Other files use the same join: open them with os.ReadFile or your own loader. Relative image paths are not resolved against the resource directory.

95.content: fonts lists OpenType files. The CLI copies them into fonts/ inside the resource directory and registers them before the first window opens. Use the font family name in styles. Fonts are not a replacement for resources/ : an image or JSON file still belongs in that directory or in the extra resources list.

96.content: Ship signed automatic updates for macOS, Windows, and Linux. Import github.com/egoist/quickgui/extensions/updater to include automatic updates. Apps that do not import it do not ship the updater.

97.content: Generate a signing key pair: Keep the private .key out of version control. Copy the .pub contents into config: {target} expands to values such as darwin-arm64 . Release notes are optional plain text, up to 16 KiB. The CLI embeds the version, identifier, feed URL, and public key. Secret keys are never embedded. App Store and sandboxed builds should exclude the updater import with a Go build tag.

98.content: Start after native.Run is ready, outside components. Share one updater for the whole app. Call updates.Check(done) from a Check for Updates item, updates.Install(done) from an available-update banner, and updates.SetAutomaticChecks(enabled, done) from settings. Callbacks run on the UI goroutine. State() returns the latest event. Options can override the feed URL and public key. Development builds are disabled by default. Use AllowDevelopment: true only with a test feed and a disposable app bundle.

99.content: Event.Status is idle , checking , available , downloading , installing , or disabled . Events include version, notes, progress, the automatic-check preference, and an optional error. On macOS, Sparkle handles download, verification, installation, and relaunch. Manual checks can show Sparkle’s standard UI; scheduled checks can feed an in-app banner. Windows and Linux check once at launch when automatic checking is enabled. QuitRequired means a helper is waiting for the app to exit. Call native.App.Quit(false, nil) after saving work. If quit is cancelled, the helper times out and leaves the current app in place.

100.content: Platform Update payload Installation macOS ZIP containing the signed .app Sparkle, included only with the updater Windows NSIS .exe installer A helper waits for exit, runs the verified installer silently, then relaunches Linux Type-2 .AppImage A helper waits for exit and replaces the user-owned AppImage Linux .deb packages, system binaries, and root-owned installs report disabled . Use the platform package manager there. Feeds are HTTPS Sparkle RSS appcasts with Ed25519 signatures. There is no unsigned fallback.

101.content: Put the private key in QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY (or SPARKLE_PRIVATE_KEY ). Alternatively, updates.ed25519SecretKey points to a local key file. The CLI signs the artifact and writes appcast-<target>.xml . Upload the versioned artifact first, then replace the feed. Each architecture has its own feed. updates.manifest = true generates a feed on every production build. macOS archives should contain a Developer ID signed, notarized app. Windows needs makensis . Linux needs appimagetool .

102.content: From this repository, build the updater once with bun packages/native/build.ts --extension updater . Packaged apps include the updater automatically when the Go import is present. See the updater example . Sparkle’s own docs cover appcast details: Sparkle .

103.content: Share Go components or add a native service your app can call. Extensions can provide ordinary Go components, retained native components, or asynchronous native services. Editor, Markdown, and Terminal are optional native component packages; Updater is an optional service. All use the same public registration boundary. Third-party extensions need no changes to quickgui-host .

104.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Choose an extension type
104.content: What you are adding What you ship Components or application logic A Go module A native service or optional backend A Go package, a manifest, and a native library Retained native UI A component SDK library and Go bindings Consumers import your Go package. The CLI finds the manifest and bundles the matching native artifact.

105.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Create an extension project
105.content: go is the default and scaffolds a reusable component. zig and rust scaffold a native service with a typed Go wrapper, a manifest, and an npm artifact package. Every template includes cmd/demo and quickgui.toml : Use --module github.com/acme/my-service for the Go module and --npm-package @acme/extension-my-service for the artifact package. Zig templates need Zig 0.16.x. From this checkout, run bun packages/cli/src/cli.ts init-extension until the CLI is published.

106.content: Export component functions from your own module. This package needs no native manifest. Publish with Go version tags. Consumers add it with go get . Importing terminal or updater still opts an app into those native packages, so keep optional integrations in separate packages.

107.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Lay out a native extension
107.content: The first-party packages in extensions/ are each both a Go module and an npm package. Keep Rust in src/ and TypeScript bindings in js/ . You can use the same layout for your own combined package: C, C++, Rust, and other languages with a C ABI can implement extensions. Rust component libraries depend on quickgui-extension-sdk , not on the renderer or quickgui-host . Implement Component and ComponentFactory ; ComponentRuntime supplies the lifecycle table. The extension owns its name, component names, properties, and release version.

108.content: Place this manifest beside the imported Go package’s source : Names start with a lowercase letter and contain at most 64 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. host is reserved. The library field is quickgui_ plus the name with hyphens replaced by underscores. The Go package records the requirement and exposes a typed call: Call operations after native.Run is ready. For a persistent service, native.OpenExtension(name, options, changed, ready) returns a session. Close it on the UI goroutine when the owner is disposed. The CLI discovers manifests through go list -deps . Both the manifest and RequireExtension are required: one controls bundling, the other controls loading.

109.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Implement the native contract
109.content: Export quickgui_extension_v1 with C linkage and a descriptor containing your name, independent version, ABI version 1 , and one of the generic function tables. A component table has create , update , render , event , and destroy ; a service table has invoke and shutdown . A component retains an opaque instance and renders the SDK's primitive tree. Stable node keys preserve focus, selection, and scrolling. Virtual lists request only visible rows plus overscan. Input returns to the package; emitted events reach its Go binding. Calls on an instance are serialized on the native UI thread. Move slow work to a worker and wake only that instance when its data changes. Return unchanged for equivalent props, and release state and wake handles on destruction. A Go wrapper can mount any registered component: See the independently compiled C counter for a complete component descriptor and lifecycle. Component frames are bounded to 16 MiB; frontend property JSON is bounded to 12 MiB. For a service , copy any borrowed request bytes before keeping them, return quickly, and reply later. Request What the extension does A one-shot method such as echo Reply once start Open a session and keep its event sink A command such as send Find that session and reply to this command stop Cancel that session shutdown Cancel every session without blocking Request and reply payloads are each limited to 64 KiB. The C echo implementation is a complete one-shot example.

110.content: The app loads each selected library at startup and checks its name, version, and ABI. Conflicting versions of the same name fail. Images stay loaded for the process lifetime; your shutdown function must cancel remaining sessions.

111.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Build and package artifacts
111.content: Build the native library for each host you support and stage it under lib/<platform>-<arch>/ . Publish that folder as an npm package whose version matches the manifest. If the npm package includes TypeScript bindings, export js/index.ts . Declare @quickgui/* runtime packages and Solid as peer dependencies, with development copies in devDependencies , not runtime dependencies . Keep the package README to build instructions; publish the user guide on your website. Helper files go next to the library. Declare their basenames in a manifest resources object keyed by darwin , linux , or windows .

112.content: Consumers go get your module and run quickgui dev . The CLI fetches the matching npm package, or you can set QUICKGUI_EXTENSION_DIR to a local artifact directory while developing. Confirm that an app without the import does not bundle the extension, that adding the import includes it, and that closing sessions stops events. End users receive the packaged app; they do not need Bun or a native toolchain to run it.

113.content: View ui.View() *Element Child Child(child any) *Element Child appends content and returns this element. Content can be an element, native node, scalar, accessor, or node-returning construction callback. Children Children(children ...any) *Element Children appends multiple children in order without replacing existing content. It also accepts []any, []*Element, and []*native.Node slices as arguments. Read the retained child nodes through element.Node.Children. Style Style(style StyleBuilder) *Element Style merges a reusable style. Scalar accessors retain independent native bindings. OnClick OnClick(handler func()) *Element OnClick handles a click without an unused event parameter. Ref Ref(handler func(*native.Node)) *Element Ref exposes the native handle once at this point in the declaration chain. Padding Padding(value any) *Element Padding sets the corresponding style property. BackgroundColor BackgroundColor(value any) *Element BackgroundColor sets the corresponding style property. 134.content: A retained native code editor with syntax coloring, line numbers, indentation, and both-axis scrolling. No language grammars are included by default. Register a linked grammar in Rust, or load one portable pack of selected Tree-sitter Wasm grammars and queries using loadLanguagePack (TypeScript) / LoadLanguagePack (Go). Unstyled by default: text and line-number colors inherit, and the component adds no background, border, rounding, padding, or syntax/diff palette. Supply application styles and explicit colors to opt into an appearance.
134.keywords: Primitives Value Language LineNumbers TabSize ReadOnly OnChange

137.content: Language selects a registered Tree-sitter grammar and highlight query. Query captures map through SyntaxTheme to eight foreground-only paint classes, so color never changes text metrics. Source or language changes reparse the bounded document; palette changes only remap retained captures, and scrolling does no syntax work. Parsing is limited to 2 MiB, individual lines over 32 KiB stay plain, and the capture count is capped. This does not require a language server.

A transition animates a change on an existing node. ui.Show removes children immediately; it does not wait for a fade-out. Opacity zero still receives layout and input. For dialogs, EnterDuration and ExitDuration control how long closing content stays mounted. See Dialog . Transitions follow the system Reduce Motion setting. Set native.WindowOptions.ReduceMotion to override it for one window.

Add a menu-bar or notification-area icon, and mark macOS template images by filename or flag. A tray icon lives in the macOS menu bar, the Windows notification area, or a Linux StatusNotifierItem host. Put the artwork in resources/ and create the icon after startup. This is separate from the packaged App Icon .

Add a square PNG that is at least 256×256 pixels at resources/icon.png . 1024×1024 is a good source. quickgui build resizes it to every size macOS, Windows, and Linux need. The CLI writes .icns for macOS, .ico for the Windows installer, and the Freedesktop hicolor sizes for Linux. Development reloads skip generated containers; production builds and a configured macos.icon still install an icon. Optional resources/icon.iconset/icon_<n>x<n>.png files replace a generated size with a hand-drawn one. That folder is a build input and is not copied into the packaged app. Set icon in the CLI config only when the source PNG lives somewhere other than resources/icon.png .

Build the native library for each host you support and stage it under lib/<platform>-<arch>/ . Publish that folder as an npm package whose version matches the manifest. If the npm package includes TypeScript bindings, export js/index.ts . Declare @quickgui/* runtime packages and Solid as peer dependencies, with development copies in devDependencies , not runtime dependencies . Keep the package README to build instructions; publish the user guide on your website. Helper files go next to the library. Declare their basenames in a manifest resources object keyed by darwin , linux , or windows .

Buttons take OnClick(func() { ... }) . Use OnClickEvent when you need *native.Event . Compound callbacks include the typed value and, when relevant, the event. Keep UI updates on the UI goroutine; use ui.Async for background work.

Create a signal with ui.CreateSignal . Read it in text and properties: ui.Text("Count: ", count()) , .Width(width()) . Event handlers batch writes automatically. initial := count() is a snapshot. Read the signal again later when the value should stay live. You can also pass a signal as a child: ui.Text("Count: ", count) keeps the prefix and updates only the number. Custom components take ordinary int , string , and struct arguments. LineItem(product, quantity()) stays subscribed to quantity .
Create an instance, then compose its named parts. Strings work as children. Configure behavior on the instance and styles on its parts. Nest parts the way you nest any other children.

DiffView uses the same registered Tree-sitter grammars as Editor. When its document, language, or syntax palette changes, the Rust core parses each visible old/new file lane once and assigns capture fragments to logical rows. Styled text is materialized and cached only when a row is mounted, with inline addition/deletion emphasis merged at non-overlapping byte boundaries. Scrolling never invokes the parser.

Each file keeps its path relative to resources/ . resources/hero.png is installed as hero.png . resources/copy/template.txt is installed as copy/template.txt . Destination names must not replace reserved names such as fonts , AppIcon.icns , quickgui.json , or the host shared library. quickgui dev and quickgui build both stage these files. A missing extra path listed in config fails the build. The resources/ directory itself is optional.

entry is the Go package to build. The config file is for the CLI; it is not loaded by the running app. You can use quickgui.toml instead: The CLI reads quickgui.toml before quickgui.config.ts . Pass --config configs/dev.toml to choose a file. Quote version values, for example version = "..." . The application icon comes from resources/icon.png . Extra files can be listed in resources . Bundle custom fonts with fonts . See App Icon and Bundled Resources .

Event.Status is idle , checking , available , downloading , installing , or disabled . Events include version, notes, progress, the automatic-check preference, and an optional error. On macOS, Sparkle handles download, verification, installation, and relaunch. Manual checks can show Sparkle’s standard UI; scheduled checks can feed an in-app banner. Windows and Linux check once at launch when automatic checking is enabled. QuitRequired means a helper is waiting for the app to exit. Call native.App.Quit(false, nil) after saving work. If quit is cancelled, the helper times out and leaves the current app in place.

Every component returns *ui.Element . Pass children with .Child(...) or .Children(...) . Return ui.Fragment(...) for several siblings without a wrapper. A plain Go if or for runs only while the component is being built. It will not update later.

Export component functions from your own module. This package needs no native manifest. Publish with Go version tags. Consumers add it with go get . Importing terminal or updater still opts an app into those native packages, so keep optional integrations in separate packages.

Export quickgui_extension_v1 with C linkage and a descriptor containing your name, independent version, ABI version 1 , and one of the generic function tables. A component table has create , update , render , event , and destroy ; a service table has invoke and shutdown . A component retains an opaque instance and renders the SDK's primitive tree. Stable node keys preserve focus, selection, and scrolling. Virtual lists request only visible rows plus overscan. Input returns to the package; emitted events reach its Go binding. Calls on an instance are serialized on the native UI thread. Move slow work to a worker and wake only that instance when its data changes. Return unchanged for equivalent props, and release state and wake handles on destruction. A Go wrapper can mount any registered component: See the independently compiled C counter for a complete component descriptor and lifecycle. Component frames are bounded to 16 MiB; frontend property JSON is bounded to 12 MiB. For a service , copy any borrowed request bytes before keeping them, return quickly, and reply later. Request What the extension does A one-shot method such as echo Reply once start Open a session and keep its event sink A command such as send Find that session and reply to this command stop Cancel that session shutdown Cancel every session without blocking Request and reply payloads are each limited to 64 KiB. The C echo implementation is a complete one-shot example.

fonts lists OpenType files. The CLI copies them into fonts/ inside the resource directory and registers them before the first window opens. Use the font family name in styles. Fonts are not a replacement for resources/ : an image or JSON file still belongs in that directory or in the extra resources list.

Generate a signing key pair: Keep the private .key out of version control. Copy the .pub contents into config: {target} expands to values such as darwin-arm64 . App Store and sandboxed builds should exclude the updater import with a Go build tag.

Keep UI in sync with signals, memos, effects, and batched updates. A component function runs once when its window (or parent) mounts. Signals keep text and properties up to date without rebuilding the whole tree.

Language selects a registered Tree-sitter grammar and highlight query. Captures map through SyntaxTheme to foreground-only spans, so highlighting does not change layout. The Rust core parses when source or language changes; scrolling only mounts logical rows and materializes their precomputed spans. Parsing is limited to 2 MiB, individual lines over 32 KiB stay plain, and the capture count is capped.

Language selects a registered Tree-sitter grammar and highlight query. Query captures map through SyntaxTheme to eight foreground-only paint classes, so color never changes text metrics. Source or language changes reparse the bounded document; palette changes only remap retained captures, and scrolling does no syntax work. Parsing is limited to 2 MiB, individual lines over 32 KiB stay plain, and the capture count is capped. This does not require a language server.

Later values override the same property. Lengths are logical pixels; strings also accept percentages. Helpers such as .FlexCol() , .P4() , .GridCols(3) , and .RoundedLg() match the TypeScript presets.

On macOS, a template image is a monochrome mask. AppKit recolors it for the menu bar's light, dark, and highlighted appearances using only the alpha channel. A filename whose stem ends in Template , optionally followed by @2x or @3x , is treated as a template: trayTemplate.png and statusTemplate@2x.png match. emailTemplateIcon.png does not. Use native.TemplateImage(path) or set ImageSource.Template when the name does not follow that convention, or to force the flag off: The same ImageSource field applies to window icons, Dock icons, about-panel icons, and menu item icons. Other platforms keep the flag and ignore it.

Pass ordinary Go values. If an argument reads a signal, that binding stays live after the function returns — you do not need extra annotations. Structs work the same way. Updating quantity changes the text; LineItem stays mounted. Start containers with ui.View() and append content with .Child(...) or .Children(...) .

Place this manifest beside the imported Go package’s source : Names start with a lowercase letter and contain at most 64 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. host is reserved. The library field is quickgui_ plus the name with hyphens replaced by underscores. The Go package records the requirement and exposes a typed call: Call operations after native.Run is ready. For a persistent service, native.OpenExtension(name, options, changed, ready) returns a session. Close it on the UI goroutine when the owner is disposed. The CLI discovers manifests through go list -deps . Both the manifest and RequireExtension are required: one controls bundling, the other controls loading.

The app loads each selected library at startup and checks its name, version, and ABI. Conflicting versions of the same name fail. Images stay loaded for the process lifetime; your shutdown function must cancel remaining sessions.
The component reference covers forms, overlays, menus, tables, trees, and more. Run the gallery from this repository:
The concealed native editor with the same controlled contract as TextField.
The confirmation-focused dialog variant with stricter backdrop-dismissal defaults.
The files in a QuickGUI Go project and how to configure them. A Go project keeps application code in a Go module and development commands in a small Bun package.

The first-party packages in extensions/ are each both a Go module and an npm package. Keep Rust in src/ and TypeScript bindings in js/ . You can use the same layout for your own combined package: C, C++, Rust, and other languages with a C ABI can implement extensions. Rust component libraries depend on quickgui-extension-sdk , not on the renderer or quickgui-host . Implement Component and ComponentFactory ; ComponentRuntime supplies the lifecycle table. The extension owns its name, component names, properties, and release version.
The host appears after the owner window is shown and closes when it is removed. Declare reverse-hosted children inside the callback so they belong to that embedded surface.

The indicator is unstyled. This example keeps its outline mounted and shows the SVG only when checked. Set ReadOnly: true to preserve focus while preventing value changes from pointer or keyboard activation.
The multiline text-editing primitive, with the same controlled value contract as Input.
The NSHostingView-backed leaf that mounts one SwiftUI component tree inside QuickGUI.

The packaged icon is the application identity. A window can show a different image on Windows and X11: iconPath is an absolute filesystem path. Join it from GetPaths as shown in Bundled Resources . After the window exists, call window.SetIcon(source) or window.ClearIcon() . On macOS, windows do not have their own icon. Use native.Desktop.SetDockIcon(&native.ImageSource{Path: iconPath}) to replace the Dock image for this process. Pass nil to restore the bundled icon. Menu-bar and notification-area icons are a different image. See Tray Icon .
The SwiftUI popover uses a native trigger. Its content can host QuickGUI children.

The tray menu is a native context menu. Action items call Click . Listen for click , double-click , enter , move , leave , menu-item , and scroll on OnEvent . ShowMenu opens the menu at the cursor on macOS and Windows. Linux hosts own menu presentation and reject that call.

ui.Input and ui.TextArea are native text editors. Bind Value and update it from OnInput . OnSubmit handles Return in a single-line input.

ui.Style() returns a value. Methods return a new value, so a shared style is never mutated. Assign the result when you derive a variation. .When(condition, style) applies extra styles while the condition is true. For a reactive condition, pass a getter: .When(selected, ui.Style().Bg("#2563eb")) . Passing width() during setup captures the current number; pass width (the getter) when it should stay live.
ui.SwiftUI.QuickGUIHostView hosts a QuickGUI subtree. Give it a size and declare children in the callback.
ui.UseRouter() exposes Navigate , Replace , Back , and Forward . ui.Link declares a target. Push adds a history entry; replace updates the current one.
Use .Hover(...) , .Active(...) , .FocusStyle(...) , .DisabledStyle(...) , and .SelectedStyle(...) . Add .Transition(...) on the base style to animate paint changes. See Transitions & Animation .

Use resources/icon.png as the packaged application icon, or change the window or Dock icon at runtime. The packaged application icon is the image Finder, the Dock, the Windows taskbar, Start Menu, and Linux desktop launchers show for your app. Put a PNG at resources/icon.png . You can also change a window icon or the macOS Dock icon while the app is running.

Use the resources config option to merge extra files or folders into the same packaged directory. Each extra path is copied under its basename. Do not list the project resources/ folder here; it is included automatically. legal/NOTICE.txt is installed as NOTICE.txt . vendor/data is installed as data/ .

Use the typed native APIs for dialogs, clipboard, shell, appearance, menus, notifications, and other platform features. Operations that return a result use a completion callback — handle errors there instead of blocking. Tray icons are covered in Tray Icon . For background work, ui.Async cancels when its component is disposed. native.Dispatch delivers a result back to the UI goroutine. Read and write signals only there. Independent native packages use native.InvokeExtension and native.OpenExtension . See Authoring Extensions .

Use these when you already have a platform container: resources/icon.icns is used on macOS when macos.icon is omitted. resources/icon.ico is used by the NSIS installer when windows.icon is omitted. linux.icon is a square PNG used when both resources/icon.png and icon are omitted. macos.icon must be an .icns . windows.icon is an .ico . These config paths override the files in resources/ . Document-type icons are a basename inside the packaged resources. See Bundled Resources .

Use ui.CreateEffect for work outside the tree, such as a subscription or a window title. It runs after mount and again when a value it read changes. ui.OnCleanup runs before the next execution and when the component goes away. Update text and properties directly. Do not rebuild UI inside an effect.
Use ui.CreateMemo for a value computed from other signals.

Use ui.For for a list that can change. Give each row a stable, unique key — a database ID, not its index. ui.KeyedFor also gives the row an accessor to the current item. Pass a new slice when you edit data. Mutating the stored slice in place does not notify subscribers. For long lists, use VirtualList or Table .
Use ui.Route for pages and ui.Layout for shared chrome. ui.Outlet is where the matched child renders.
Use ui.Show to mount or remove children from state.

Use ui.TransitionDeclaration when several properties share one timing. Field Usage .TransitionProperty(...) Property names, as a comma-separated string or []string . .TransitionDuration(...) A number of milliseconds, a time.Duration , or "180ms" / "0.18s" . Durations are limited to 0–10 seconds. .TransitionEasing(...) "linear" , "ease" , "ease-in" , "ease-out" , or "ease-in-out" . .TransitionMaxFps(...) Optional frame-rate cap. Omit it to follow the display. A node has one duration, easing, and frame-rate cap for all selected properties. Delays, cubic-bezier() , and per-property timings are not supported. ui.Style().Transition(180 * time.Millisecond) animates background, border, and text colors. "all" includes every supported paint property. "none" removes the shorthand.

View , Text , Button , and Input cover most layout and text. Chain styles, properties, and handlers on the same element. The optional extensions/editor package adds the Rust-core Editor , CodeBlock , and DiffView surfaces without CGO or another native library. The optional extensions/markdown package adds retained Markdown , including streaming reconciliation and CodeBlock rendering.
